Part A — Creating Data Frames
 
```{r}
  
# Create vectors
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

# Combine into data frame
students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
students

# Check column types
typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)

# Create courses data frame directly
courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)
courses
``` 
 
Question #1
All columns must be the same length because each row is one complete record. Every piece of data about one person has to line up. If lengths don't match, R gives an error because it doesn't know how to fit them together.
 
Question #2
A data frame works like a list. Each column is separate, so each can be a different type — text, numbers, or TRUE/FALSE. But inside one column, all values come from the same group, so they must all be the same type.
 
 
 
Part B — Subsetting Data Frames
 
```{r}
  
# Access age column
students$age
students[["age"]]
students["age"]

# Access 2nd row
students[2, ]

# Access row 3, name column
students[3, "name"]

# Rows where passed is TRUE
students[students$passed == TRUE, ]

# Passed is TRUE AND age > 19
students[students$passed == TRUE & students$age > 19, ]
 
``` 
Question #3
 students$age  gives just the values as a simple list.  students["age"]  keeps it as a small data frame — still a table with column names. Use  $  or  [[ ]]  when you just want the values, and  [ ]  when you want to keep the table structure.
 
Question #4
 &  means both conditions must be true at the same time. It checks every row and only keeps rows where both are TRUE. If you use  |  instead, it keeps rows where at least one condition is true — even if the other one is false.
 
 
 
Part C — Data Frame Properties
 
```{r}
  
# Structure
str(students)

# Dimensions
dim(students)
nrow(students)
ncol(students)

# Column names
names(students)
colnames(students)

# Summary
summary(students)
 
``` 
Question #5
For numbers, summary shows the smallest, largest, and average values. For TRUE/FALSE, it just counts how many of each there are. For text like names, there's no average or minimum, so it just tells you the type and length.
 
Question #6
Use  str()  when you want to see what type each column is and how the data is organized. Use  summary()  when you want a quick look at the values themselves — like knowing the average age or how many passed.
 
 
 
Part D — Data Frame Operations
 
```{r}
  
# Add year_level column
students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)
students

# Remove passed column
students$passed <- NULL
students

# Sort by age ascending
students[order(students$age), ]

# Sort by age descending
students[order(-students$age), ]
 
``` 
Question #7
No — R would say that column doesn't exist anymore. Once you set a column to  NULL , it's gone. Always remember what your data looks like after each step — you can't use something you've already deleted.
 
Question #8
 order()  doesn't change your data. It just gives you a list that says which row comes first, second, and so on. When you use that list inside the brackets, R reads it like a guide and rebuilds the table in that new order.
 
 
 
Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
 
```{r}
  
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

# Add average column
grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

# Add remarks column
grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")

# Show only Failed rows with name and average
grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
 
``` 
Question #9
I would make a new column showing the difference between midterm and final scores. Then I'd compare two groups: students who already had low midterm scores, and students who started okay but dropped a lot. I'd sort both groups by their final average and see which one generally ended up with lower marks.
 
 
 
Conclusion
 
A data frame is R's main way to store table-style data. It's made by putting vectors of the same length together. Each column can be a different type, but all columns must be the same length. This makes it perfect for real-world data like grades, surveys, or lists of information.

